title: IR Remote Control Replacement
subtitle: TM4C123GXL (ARM Cortex-M4)
summary: A bare-metal universal IR remote that records and replays signals from any consumer remote via a UART command shell — every driver written at the register level, with no vendor HAL.
coverAlt: Captured IR mark/space waveform with a 38 kHz carrier inset
highlights: Wrote all drivers — clock, UART0, timers, NVIC — directly against the datasheet with no vendor HAL.
Chose raw mark/space timing capture over protocol decoding, making the system remote-agnostic.
Generated the 38 kHz carrier with Timer0B PWM, gated at runtime by switching a pin between GPIO and alternate function.

sections.heading: Remote-agnostic by design
sections.body: Rather than decoding a fixed set of protocols (NEC, RC5, Sony), the system captures raw mark/space timing. That one decision removes the protocol table entirely — anything that transmits on a 38 kHz carrier can be recorded and replayed, including remotes whose encoding I'd never seen.

sections.heading: Microsecond capture
sections.body: Edges are captured with dual-edge input capture on Timer0A, timestamped against a free-running 32-bit counter. The free-running counter is what buys microsecond resolution without drift across a long frame — each edge is an absolute timestamp, not an accumulated delta, so error doesn't compound down the burst.

sections.heading: Carrier generation and gating
sections.body: Timer0B drives a 38 kHz PWM carrier. Gating it at runtime is done by reconfiguring the pin between GPIO and alternate-function mode — the timer keeps running while the pin decides whether the world hears it. SysTick-based gap detection marks IR frame boundaries so a burst is correctly segmented into a replayable frame.

sections.heading: Analog front end
sections.body: The IR emitter is driven through a 2N3904 transistor, since the GPIO pin alone can't source the LED current needed for usable range. Reception uses a demodulating IR receiver, which strips the carrier and hands back clean logic-level mark/space edges.

title: IEEE 754 Half-Precision Floating-Point Adder
subtitle: Intel MAX 10 FPGA
summary: A 16-bit IEEE 754 floating-point adder/subtractor designed and synthesized in SystemVerilog, wrapped in a complete keypad-to-display user-facing system.
coverAlt: FP16 bit-field layout above the add datapath, normalization shifter marked as the critical path
highlights: Implemented operand magnitude ordering, exponent-difference mantissa alignment, sign-aware add/subtract, normalization, and overflow/underflow flags.
Built the full user-facing system: 4×4 matrix keypad scanner with FSM debounce, edge-detected operand capture, and a time-multiplexed 7-segment driver.
Identified the unrolled normalization shifter as the critical path from static timing results, with pipelining as the route to closure.

sections.heading: The datapath
sections.body: Floating-point addition is mostly bookkeeping around a single integer add. Operands are ordered by magnitude so the smaller exponent is always the one shifted; the mantissa is aligned by the exponent difference; the add or subtract is selected by comparing signs; and the result is normalized back into IEEE 754 form with overflow and underflow flagged at the boundaries.

sections.heading: A full system, not just a block
sections.body: The adder is wrapped in everything needed to actually use it on the board. A 4×4 matrix keypad is scanned with an FSM that debounces mechanical bounce and decodes hex; edge detection captures each operand exactly once per press; and a time-multiplexed driver scans the 7-segment displays fast enough to look continuous.

sections.heading: Timing analysis
sections.body: Synthesis landed at 706 logic elements and 137 registers. Reading the static timing report, the critical path is the unrolled normalization shifter — an unavoidable consequence of doing a variable-length shift combinationally in a single cycle. Pipelining that shifter is the clear route to timing closure, trading one cycle of latency for a substantially higher fmax.

title: AntarLens
subtitle: AI Cognitive Health Platform
summary: A deployed full-stack AI platform that tracks focus, mood, energy and sleep, then predicts a user's cognitive patterns from their own data via a 30-second daily check-in.
coverAlt: Four tracked cognitive signals plotted over time beside a 30-second check-in ring
highlights: Architected the data model and auth on Supabase row-level security, isolating user records at the database layer.
Built a privacy-first design with encryption at rest and full user memory controls.
Predicts cognitive patterns from a user's own history rather than population averages.

sections.heading: Security at the database layer
sections.body: Auth and the data model were designed together around Supabase row-level security. User isolation is enforced by Postgres policies rather than by application code — so a bug in a route handler can't leak another user's rows, because the query itself is scoped before it ever returns.

sections.heading: Privacy as a product decision
sections.body: Cognitive health data is about as sensitive as personal data gets. The platform encrypts at rest and gives users full control over their stored memory — including the ability to inspect and delete what the system retains about them.

sections.heading: Low-friction input, personal baseline
sections.body: The entire input surface is a 30-second daily check-in, because adherence is the real constraint on any self-tracking product. Predictions are drawn from each user's own accumulated history, so the baseline is personal rather than a population average that may not describe them at all.

title: Kashlly
subtitle: AI Financial Management Platform
summary: A deployed AI financial tool for freelancers covering cash flow, invoicing and runway forecasting — including a real-time runway calculator that turns financial data into plain-English guidance.
coverAlt: Cash balance declining toward a runway marker, with invoice follow-up statuses
highlights: Built a real-time runway calculator that converts raw financial data into plain-English guidance.
Developed an AI pricing advisor that derives recommended rates from real expense data.
Automated invoice follow-up that drafts and sends reminder emails on overdue invoices.

sections.heading: Runway in plain English
sections.body: Freelance finances fail on interpretation, not arithmetic. The runway calculator updates in real time as figures change and states the outcome in plain language — how long the money lasts and what moves it — instead of leaving a number on screen for the user to interpret.

sections.heading: Pricing grounded in real numbers
sections.body: The AI pricing advisor derives recommended rates from the user's actual expense data rather than generic benchmarks, so the floor it suggests reflects what that specific freelancer needs to cover.

sections.heading: Chasing invoices automatically
sections.body: Overdue invoices trigger automated follow-up: the system drafts and sends reminder emails without the user having to write the awkward message themselves — removing the social friction that causes freelancers to delay chasing payment.

title: Network Security Project
subtitle: Group Lead
summary: Led a team designing and presenting a network security solution, coordinating task assignments and deadlines through to faculty recognition for the team's contribution.
coverAlt: Network topology split by a filtering boundary into untrusted and segmented zones
highlights: Led the team through design and final presentation of a network security solution.
Coordinated task assignments and deadlines across the group.
Received faculty recognition for the team's contribution.

sections.heading: Leading the design
sections.body: As group lead I owned both the technical direction of the security solution and the schedule that got it delivered — breaking the design into assignable pieces, setting internal deadlines ahead of the real one, and keeping the final presentation coherent across contributors.

sections.heading: Recognition
sections.body: The team's work received faculty recognition for its contribution — the practical validation that the design held up under review.
